title: Apixaban and DOAC Safety
bottomLine: Apixaban directly inhibits factor Xa and increases bleeding risk, but it is not routinely titrated by INR. Nursing priorities are bleeding assessment, last-dose timing, adherence, renal/hepatic and interaction review, and urgent escalation of major bleeding or neurologic change.
recognize: Severe headache or focal neurologic change
differentiate: Routine INR does not show a therapeutic apixaban target
Minor bruising differs from major hemorrhage with instability or critical-organ symptoms
workup: Targeted imaging/labs for suspected major bleeding
management: Interruption/reversal only through the individualized emergency/procedural plan
medicationSafety: Do not use INR to titrate apixaban
Do not stop casually before procedures
redFlags: Severe headache or new neurologic deficit
counselling: Report black stool, hematemesis, hematuria and neurologic symptoms
Follow drug-specific missed-dose and procedure instructions
followUp: Bleeding/adherence and renal-function review when indicated
examTrap: Using INR to decide whether apixaban is therapeutic.
oneLinePearl: DOAC means different monitoring, not no monitoring.

title: Digoxin Toxicity
bottomLine: Digoxin has a narrow safety margin. New nausea, anorexia, confusion, visual change or dysrhythmia—especially with renal decline, dehydration or low potassium—should trigger toxicity assessment and dose review.
recognize: Bradycardia, heart block or other dysrhythmia
Renal decline or electrolyte disturbance increases risk
differentiate: A serum digoxin concentration must be interpreted with timing and symptoms
Acute severe toxicity may cause hyperkalemia while chronic risk often rises with hypokalemia
assessment: Drug interactions and recent diuretic use
management: Withhold further dose and escalate according to order/protocol when toxicity suspected
Prepare digoxin immune Fab for severe life-threatening toxicity when ordered
medicationSafety: Monitor potassium after antidote because it can shift rapidly
counselling: Report new GI, visual or rhythm symptoms
examTrap: Chasing one digoxin level while ignoring the clinical rhythm and renal/electrolyte picture.
oneLinePearl: Digoxin toxicity lives at the intersection of kidneys, potassium and rhythm.

title: Lithium Toxicity
bottomLine: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is highly sensitive to kidney function, dehydration and sodium balance. New coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion or severe GI symptoms after dehydration or an interacting drug is toxicity until assessed.
recognize: Recent vomiting, diarrhea, fever, heat exposure or medication interaction
differentiate: A stable mild fine tremor can be a chronic adverse effect; new coarse tremor/ataxia is more concerning
Lithium toxicity can mimic worsening psychiatric or neurologic illness
assessment: NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretic and other interaction review
management: Hold/escalate suspected toxicity according to plan
Prepare toxicology/nephrology/dialysis management in severe cases
medicationSafety: NSAIDs and selected antihypertensives/diuretics can raise lithium exposure
Avoid abrupt major sodium/fluid changes without guidance
counselling: Maintain consistent hydration/sodium intake according to plan
Seek advice during vomiting, diarrhea or febrile illness
examTrap: Treating coarse tremor and gait instability as harmless expected effects.
oneLinePearl: Lithium + dehydration + neuro change = toxicity assessment.

title: Methotrexate Weekly-Dose Safety
bottomLine: For many non-oncology inflammatory indications, low-dose methotrexate is once weekly—not daily. Verify the exact day and indication, monitor CBC/liver/kidney function, and urgently assess mouth ulcers, fever, bruising or new dyspnea.
recognize: Weekly dosing for many inflammatory indications
differentiate: Oncology regimens can differ—never generalize one schedule across indications
Mild nausea differs from severe mucositis with fever or cytopenia
assessment: CBC, liver and renal monitoring status
Mouth, infection, bleeding and respiratory symptoms
workup: Targeted lung assessment if dyspnea develops
management: Hold/escalate serious toxicity according to the treatment plan
Treat infection/cytopenias and adjust for organ dysfunction as ordered
medicationSafety: Daily-vs-weekly errors can cause catastrophic toxicity
Renal impairment and interacting drugs increase exposure
counselling: Do not add doses for pain
examTrap: Assuming methotrexate is a daily medication because most pills are daily.
oneLinePearl: Methotrexate: say the day of the week before you give the dose.

title: Gentamicin Toxicity and Monitoring
bottomLine: Gentamicin can be effective for selected serious infections but can injure renal tubules and the inner ear. Dose/interval depend on weight, renal function and protocol; drug levels are only useful when collected at the correct time.
recognize: Rising creatinine or falling urine output
Risk with prolonged exposure, dehydration or concurrent nephrotoxins
differentiate: Infection-related AKI and gentamicin nephrotoxicity can coexist
Vestibular toxicity can present as imbalance even without hearing loss
assessment: Weight and renal function used for dosing
management: Adjust/stop under prescriber/pharmacy direction for toxicity
medicationSafety: Incorrectly timed levels can mislead dosing
Renal decline requires rapid dose/interval review
counselling: Report hearing, ringing or balance changes promptly
followUp: Renal and auditory recovery monitoring when toxicity occurs
examTrap: Drawing a gentamicin level at the wrong time and treating the number as valid.
oneLinePearl: Gentamicin: right dose, right interval, right level time, watch kidneys and ears.
